projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Jefferson Gene Bell was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Tualatin, Oregon. It's November 14, 2007. We're talking to Jeff Bell who is a resident of Tualatin. How long have you lived in Tualatin, Jeff?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Since 1964.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: 1964, but we're going to go back to a period of your life when you were a young man and how you enlisted or were drafted into the military back in the 1940s when the Great War, as it's called, began and much of America got involved in that either on the home front or overseas in various parts of the world. So, let's go back in time until your high school years, maybe. Tell us about that period and how you were brought into the war effort.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I was going to high school at Stevenson, Washington and I came to Portland to work. After leaving school, I was welding in Albina Shipyards when I was drafted by the Army and asked to report to Fort Lewis, Washington.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: What year was that?

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: How old were you then?

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: 19, but you had finished high school?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I didn't finish, I quit in the middle of my senior year to go to work in the shipyards.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Because everyone was involved in the effort, right, in those days?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yeah. A strange thing happened, then. My brother-in-law entered the service at the same time and the 2 of us were sent to Fort Lewis, Washington along with 625 other draftees and out of the 625 that processed through Fort Lewis, Washington, 2 of us were sent to Fort Knox, Kentucky. It was my future brother-in-law, Howard Clark and I, was the two that got selected to go to Fort Knox, Kentucky to the tank divisions.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: How were you selected for the tank division?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Through our resumes that we had to fill out and prepare for what we had been doing and experiences. Both of us were mechanical.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: So, that was a good field then. They needed a lot of those people at that time.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: What was Fort Knox like?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, it was very warm and muggy when we were there taking our basic training, but we had a good time there. When we got through with basic training, the 2 of us were selected for advanced schooling in mechanics. So, we were stationed there for another 26 weeks which seemed like an eternity. His wife came back and got an apartment in Louisville and my fiance came back eventually and we got married in Louisville.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: You could live in town in an apartment and just be at the job from 8:30 in the morning until 4:30 everyday just like a job. That sounded like forever. When we were going to be there for 26 weeks. So, we got married in Louisville. [Time Elapsed 3:52] Camp Breckinridge, Kentucky and Fort Ord, California Amphibious Tractor Training

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: That's great and then what happened?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, we finished our training and they sent us to Camp Breckinridge in Kentucky to a tank division. We trained there for a period of time and they took us out of there and put us on trains and shipped me and my group to Fort Ord, California and put us in the amphibious tractors which were new at that time.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Could you describe an amphibious tractor?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, it's kind of like a tank, but instead of being armored and heavy guns, they are more like just a boat that you put 23 people inside of. They are quite high. They are like 10 feet high and probably 25 or 30 feet long. They float on the water and they also run on shore. They have (2) 30 caliber machine guns on the back and (2) 50s on the front corners. So, they are heavily armored with weapons and haul the troops to shore off of the LSTs.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: LSTs stand for what?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: That's Landing Ship, Tanks. They're 420 feet long. So, they haul quite a few of those amphibious tractors. They have bow doors that open and ramps that drop down and you run out into the ocean.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: So, your training next was on this amphibious tractor and your job was what?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I was a mechanic. So, I had to keep them running and repairs and broken parts and whatnot. [Time Elapsed 5:53] Hawaii to Leyte Island in the Philippines

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: So, how long were you there?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: We was in Hawaii for probably around 4 months training on those. Then, we left Hawaii and sailed for 30 days getting to Leyte for our first operation.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Leyte in the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Leyte Island in the Philippines. We were the first troops to go ashore there. We were the third wave of troops to land on Leyte Island. [Time Elapsed 6:28] MacArthur's Return to the Philippines

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: That was at what period in the war? What had happened in the Philippines earlier?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: The Japanese had the Philippine Islands at that time and MacArthur had went to another island for security. Then, he said, "We shall return." And he did. That's when we went ashore.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: So, he was in charge of the whole effort?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yes. All of the South Pacific Operations, he was in charge of.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Did you personally see him?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yes, I seen him walk ashore.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Can you describe that day?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, all I can remember is we was kind of amazed that he waded ashore on the island when actually there was ramps that had been pushed out to the LSTs so the trucks could haul supplies ashore.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Maybe it was more dramatic? Made better news film?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I guess so. Yes.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Can you describe the kind of military action that was going on? Did that just begin a whole process of heavy fighting?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yes, it did. When we hit the shore, we ran up against a log with our "amphib" and one of the medics--we hauled 23 medics ashore. One of the Lieutenants was handling the winch that lets the tail gate down so you can walk out. He just cranked it wide open and it went so fast that it let the cable get out of the winch which has got a steel plate around it to protect the--keep the cable in. It got out between that so we couldn't move. I was a mechanic. So, I had to get on top of that thing and unbolt that winch and take it out of there and take a chisel hammer and drive that cable back in where it belonged and put it back in and bolt it down. All the time, bullets were flying by and shells were popping. Limbs were falling out of the trees.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: When I got that bolted back down, they said, "Well, let's see how far up the front we can go." So, we backed away from that log and went around, went ahead about 100 yards and the Marines or the military men stopped us. They said, "We've got a machine gun set up here in case of counter attack. Get that tank back out of here." So, we backed up a little and just parked. Got out and was standing around. We hadn't much more than got parked and 2 bombs came--shells came out of the mountains. One hit right in front of me about 50 yards. It killed 5 of our guys. All the shrapnel went sideways, luckily for me, because I was closer than most of them. The other one--we went back carrying the wounded back to the medics who had set up right behind us. There was the other shell hole right between our tracks where we'd been sitting 10 minutes before. So, the Good Lord had his hand over me, I think.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: So, you're on shore, now. What happens after that?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, after about 4 days, the island we got pretty well secured except for up in the mountains. We went around the island and made a landing in the bay to chase out a few Japs that were living on ships that had been bombarded and sunk in the bay. We cleared them out.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It wasn't too long after that, we loaded up on LSTs again and took the 1st Marine Division and took them to Okinawa to make a landing there. Along the way, we hit a typhoon. Actually, there was several Navy ships that were sunk. I think there was a couple of Navy destroyers. One cruiser broke in two. Fortunately for us, we were on the fringe of the typhoon with the LST. I had to go down in the basement and make sure the amphibious tractors were secured yet and not sliding around because we were tipping so far, the waves would come up halfway up on the cabin.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I went and made my way down at the back of the ship and the front would go clear out of sight it was going up and down so far in those waves. So, I was really afraid we would never make it through that storm, but we did and we landed the Marines on Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: This was what year?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It was still in '44.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: 1944? So, you were still in the South Pacific, then?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I'm not sure. It might've been in '45 because Okinawa was fairly close to Japan. We secured the island there. They loaded us back up on LSTs, again, and gave us maps and was going to send us to the back side of Japan--our outfit--and get their attention back there. Then, the main force was going to go in Tokyo Harbor.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: So, dropped the bomb. That stopped that. They signed the peace. They held us on those ships for about 2 weeks and they decided to send us back to Mindoro to clean up the island--take the military stuff off the island.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Mindoro is where? In the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: In the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: So, we really sweated it out. We had a Japanese sub chasing us all the way back. So, we thought, "Boy, this would be terrible. The war is-the peace is signed and here we are going to get chased down and shot by a submarine."

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: How did you know about the submarine?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, U-boats--our little sub chasers were running around out there dropping depth charges like crazy most of the way back.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Talk about life during your time in the Pacific. What was daily life like?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, I don't know, it was just rather routine. Work on the machines that needed work. We were really very fortunate again there, I was anyhow, and most everybody else was. About the first three or four days, we just camped where ever we parked our "amphib". We put up 2 or 3 pup tents and just slept in them. Our particular machine was broke down. So, when they decided to put up the company tents all in one area about a quarter of a mile from where we were at, we moved in there and that very night a Japanese bomber came in. We were right between 2 airports, Kadena and Naha [Okinawa] Airports. This Jap bomber came in and started dropping bombs. Each one would get a little closer and a little louder. He dropped 6 bombs and the last one wasn't probably 100 yards from our tent area.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Then next day, we went up to where our "amphib" was parked and it had 60 some holes blown through it. So, we were really fortunate we weren't still there. 10

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Did that "amphib" ever get going again?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: So, you had to have other ways of getting around.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yeah. What was really sad to me was the DUKW, the truck that runs on the water, coming ashore with Navy personnel rounded up in those things that had been killed by the kamikaze planes out in the bay. They lost more sailors than they did Army and Marines put together because of the kamikaze planes.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: That was where? In what bay?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: So, you were hauling away the dead?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: They were, the Navy was, and they buried them up there on Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Again, your job was maintenance, mechanical work on anything that moved or at least the "amphibs"?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: The "amphibs", trucks.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: How was daily life in terms of food? How did you [inaudible] with that?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, it was kind of touch and go. You ate a lot of stuff out of cans and packages. When they'd get the mess tents set up, then you'd have regular food--better food.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: A lot of that was on your own.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It was. Anytime, you're camping and you don't have your main camp set up, yet, it was just eating out of C-rations.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Was there any way to keep in touch with home and family?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: No, just write letters.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: That would take how long?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I don't know, had to take a week or so or a couple of weeks for a letter to get back and forth.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Were they censored?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I suppose they were. 12

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: You don't remember if anything got taken out of your messages?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: I know you took some picture, you said, but that was harder to do in those days, right?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It was, yeah. I carried a little camera with me and I took pictures when I could.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Getting film was harder.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It was. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: In terms of people that you served with, do you remember some of those people? Are any of them still alive you keep in touch with?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: No, we don't. I never kept in touch. I got out of the service in the middle of January in '46 and I got busy working.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Can you describe what happened as you finished your work in the South Pacific. Then, you came back to the States then after cleaning up some of the stuff in Okinawa. Then, what happened?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: You mean in the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: After you finished Okinawa, then you came back to the States?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: We went back to Mindoro. We cleaned all the military stuff off of the island of Mindoro, bombs, and loaded those on ships. A lot of the stuff, they put on barges and took it out in the ocean and pushed it off with bulldozers--trucks and jeeps and all kinds of equipment and we got the island cleaned up.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: We eventually loaded up on troop ships and came back to San Francisco and rode a ship up to Seattle. Came in to Seattle.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Then, you stayed in a few more months or was that the end of your tour?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, we had to be processed out at Fort Lewis. We were there probably a week or two. Then, I came home. My wife and brother-in-law came up and all of them came up and hauled me home.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: So, you were in the Army. That was your branch even though you were running these amphibious?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It was the Amphibious Corps. I rode a ship as much as most Navy guys, but I was in the Army. 14

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: How was food on the ship?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It was pretty good. Pretty good.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: What would you do if you had any free time?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Usually just read or sleep or whatever. Play cards.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Did you get a chance to really appreciate the culture or the environment of the Philippines, for example?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It was rather amazing on Okinawa. Philippines, we didn't see anything in the way of farming, the place was so badly shot up from bombardment. In Okinawa, any place, even hillside, they would terrace off a little area and have flowers or a garden in those little areas on the mountainsides.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Did you ever have a chance to meet any of the people in these places?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: No, only in Leyte we had women that would come and take-pick up our laundry and do it.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Did you pay for that yourself?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yeah. Pay for our laundry, but it was very reasonable.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: What was, do you think the attitude of the Filipino people, for instance?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: They were very happy we were there.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Were there stories of what had happened earlier during the war, there?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yes, there sure was. The women, particularly in Tacloban area where there was a school, would tell us of the situations where the Japanese would come in and they'd line up the men and chop their heads off and throw the babies in the air and catch them on a bayonet and that type of thing. It was really saddening.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Did you, yourself, have some close calls? You mentioned some bombs falling and some other action, bullets flying at you from the mainland on the craft while you were trying to repair it. Did you have some close calls?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: That's about as close as it got.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: How about friends that you had? Did you lose some of them?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yes, I did. Two, the driver and the assistant driver, on the one amphibious tractor that got the shell dropped right beside it. The driver crawled underneath because he said, "I'm not going to make it." 16

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: He went to the priest on the ship, before we landed, and said, "I'm not going to make it." Sure enough. He crawled under that thing, but a piece of shrapnel went right under there and it went through his chest. The assistant driver laid underneath the tree about 50 feet from me and Master Sergeant in charge of maintenance came over and squatted down beside him. I started to get up and go over there, but he stood up and he seen me and came back up to where I was. So, I just squatted back down. He just started to say, "Did you see those shells hitting in the ocean out there?" He didn't even get through talking until 2 hit, the one right beside Balasco [sp] who was laying against a palm tree there. The other one hit back where we had been sitting. It was kind of scary. My hearing has never been the same since.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: I'm sure. Well, was there a follow up at home, when you got home? Speaking of your war experience, now. Was the Veterans Administration in action, then. Did they have some follow up physical medical care for you and things like that?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: No. I didn't pursue any of that because I didn't need it, I guess.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: How about the G.I. Bill?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I took advantage of that. When I first got home, I went to framing houses with my brother. We done that for a period of time until it got so cold you'd mash your finger and you wouldn't even know it until you got home and it thawed out. I decided there'd got to be something better than framing house.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Was that here in the Washington/Oregon area?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It was around 82nd Street area. We built 5 different houses there and framed them up ready for finish work. I was pretty fortunate, I got a chance to buy into New House and Hutchin's Towing Company along with 3 other [inaudible] drivers. We done that for 10 years and decided that 24 hour answering the phone was getting kind of tiresome. So, we sold out and then went into excavating for a period of time for 6 years. A friend of mine that I'd built a tow truck for had a big body shop in Redmond, Ben Jacuse [sp]. He wanted me to come and be the service manager when he got the Chevrolet Dealership. So, I sold my excavating and went to Redmond and was the service manager for a year and a half. My youngest daughter was born there in Redmond.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Good. So, your family moved around a little bit. How many children did you have?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I had four, two boys and two girls.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: After Bend in Central Oregon, what was next? You moved from Central Oregon, you said?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yeah, I moved back to Portland eventually when the service manager's job didn't pan out like he said it would. I quit him and went to driving for Bend Portland Trucking and came back to Portland.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Is that how you finished your career, in trucking?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I did. I got to driving for--pulling extra trips for Sand Tree Trucking when Bend Trucking was slow in the winter time, because I was on the bottom of the board. It was such a good job that I actually sold my dump truck. 18

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I'd came back and started excavating, again. I sold it and went to driving steady for Sand Tree Trucking and drove there for the last 22 years of my career until I retired.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: So, that was your longest stretch, right?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: That didn't slow you down. In retirement you still kept busy, right?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I got retired from there. Got talked into taking a job at Rose City Golf Course taking care of 25 golf carts for them. So, I done that for 6 years.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Golfing is still a pastime.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yes, it is. I still golf 2 or 3 times a week. I walk 9 holes just for the exercise. We don't worry about score, but we get our exercise that way.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: How old are you now, Jeff?

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: 83. What advice do you have for the younger generation, today, about any of these things we've talked about--military, finding skills and using them and continuing in a career. Any advice you'd like to offer?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, I would say the first thing people should think about is a good education. Get as much education as they can. Although, I have 2 grandchildren that are in the Air Force, a granddaughter and a grandson and my son-in-law is a retired commander from the Navy. It's his 2 children that are in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: OK. So, some of them followed grandpa in the military world.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Yeah. Granddaughter is going for Officers Candidate School.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: In the military world today, you're covered on that. What about what brought you to Tualatin? Was it when you were still trucking and still driving?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I had a house on Mt. Scott and I got the job driving for Sand Tree Trucking. It was in Tigard at that time across from Fred Meyers. So, I sold my house there and bought 2 1/2 acres on the Tualatin River and built a house in 1964. Lived there for 34 years.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: What street is that?

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Hazelbrook. Is that near the middle school, today?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It's close. It's 2 houses from the park out there, can't think of the name of the park.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Jurgens Park? 20

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Jurgens Park, right.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: So, has Tualatin been a good place to live?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: It has. It's been pretty good.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Again, how do you see thinks changing in 2000 in terms of our own involvement militarily around the world? Do you have any thought how we stand today compared to in 1943?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Well, back then it was a case of having to defend ourselves and go to war like we did.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Now, I don't agree with what they're trying to do, trying to change all them Arab nations to thinking like we do. I don't think we've got any business trying to do that at all. They've been that way for centuries. Here we are trying to convince them to do it our way. I don't think that's the thing to do.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Are there some things we haven't talked about you'd like to add today?

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Not that I can think of.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Tell me about the family, again. You are married to Marge.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: For 63 years.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: 63 years and the children are all grown and away. There's 4 of them.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: I lost my oldest son.

sp.speaker: Larry McClure
sp.p: Three [Correction: Five] grandchildren--or great grandchildren. It's been good talking to you about this. We'll put this into our files here at the Historical Society and make copies for you, too.

sp.speaker: Jefferson Gene Bell
sp.p: Thank you very much. [End of Interview]
